high_priority_articles.title: Armenia's exports to Russia raise concerns over sanctions circumvention - rapporteur.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Armenia's exports to Russia raise concerns over sanctions circumvention  rapporteur.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Despite deteriorating political relations between Armenia and Russia, bilateral trade has flourished, leaving Western partners wondering over Yerevan’s approach to sanctions.
In the aftermath of the sanctions against Moscow, Armenia’s exports to Russia tripled in 2022 and then doubled between January and August 2023, providing ground for accusations about the South Caucasus country’s compliance with the Western sanctions regime.
While the political relations of Armenia with Russia have largely deteriorated in the last few years, bilateral trade with Russia flourished.
Risky trade partner
Since Armenia’s accession in 2014 to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, Russia has become Armenia’s number one trading partner. Russia’s share in foreign exports of Armenia further increased in the aftermath of the invasion of Ukraine.
In 2023, trade with Russia accounted for over 35% of the country’s foreign trade, compared with the EU’s 13% share in the total.
The Armenian economy’s high dependency on its trade with Russia has made it practically impossible for the country to join the sanctions against Moscow without risking unprecedented economic downfall.
This growing economic dependency on the Russian market does not, however, impede the Armenian government’s attempts to slowly shift the country’s geopolitical orientation towards the West.
Quite the contrary, the tensions between the Kremlin and Yerevan, including Armenia’s open disagreement with the Kremlin’s war of aggression, continue to grow in parallel with the increase of trade numbers.
Many in Armenia are worried that the Kremlin can use Armenia’s economic dependency as political leverage, with recent opinion polls conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) showing that 40% of Armenians view Russia as the most significant political threat to their country, after Turkey and Azerbaijan.
Meanwhile, Russia has in recent months already blocked on several occasions the import of Armenian products on its ground checkpoint with Georgia.
Increase in re-exports
In 2022, the volume of trade between Armenia and Russia nearly doubled, reaching $5.3 billion, according to Armenia’s state statistics agency. This trend continued apace in 2023 and in the early months of 2024. The increase in Armenia’s exports to Russia is largely due to the re-export of products from third countries.
According to the UN Comtrade Database, the list of products exported from Armenia to Russia in the last two years includes but is not limited to, mobile phones, computers, headphones, and other technical equipment.
In recent months the re-export of diamonds and gold has also been on the rise.
To avoid possible issues with compliance with the sanctions regime, the Armenian government has made the data on trade with Russia publicly available and has invested in providing almost real-time updates on imports and exports to the Russian Federation.
“There is a rise in re-exports, the products being re-exported are not currently under sanctions, or at least not yet,” Seda Hergnyan of Hetq.am Investigative platform, specialising in monitoring Armenia’s compliance with sanctions, told Euractiv.
“However, if tomorrow the collective West decides to consider the re-exports to Russia as sanctions circumvention, all of Armenia’s exports will be put at risk, but the primary risks associated with increased re-exports are risks for Armenia’s economic development itself,” Hergnyan said
“There are growing concerns that Armenia’s economic growth rate is becoming even more dependent on the Russian market. This economic growth process is not stable and is reliant on external factors rather than internal economic development and increased production rates. These external factors can change overnight,” she cautioned.
For now, however, according to Hergnyan, the re-export process is transparent and is openly documented by Armenia’s public statistics service.
She is not the sole journalist in Armenia who agrees that the data is transparent and updated almost in real-time. This transparency is supposedly helping the Armenian government to dispel doubts regarding its intentions.
Meanwhile, to increase oversight of possible sanctions circumvention by Armenia-registered companies, the country’s authorities introduced in 2023 mandatory government licenses for shipments of microchips, transformers, video cameras, antennas, and other electronic equipment to Russia.
A contradiction of views
Since February 2022, the increased export figures are occasionally presented in Western media as proof that Armenia is deliberately helping Russia circumvent the sanctions regime.
“We regularly see waves of English language posts on X, often initiated by Azerbaijani users, that accuse Armenia of deliberately helping Russia to circumvent the sanctions,” Ani Grigoryan, the editor and founder of #CivilNetCheck, told Euractiv.
In addition, she said, some foreign experts, genuinely concerned with the compliance of third parties with sanctions against Russia, also sometimes present data on Armenia’s trade with Russia as proof of non-compliance.
“The numbers are often presented without any context or with no reference to the particularities or vulnerabilities of Armenia’s context. Even if the numbers are not fake, their representation without relevant context analysis can become a manipulation,” she said.
The accusations of Armenia’s sanctions circumvention have recently been addressed even by Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. In an interview with France 24, he stressed that neither the European Union nor the United States have any reservations regarding Armenia’s compliance with sanctions.
The US and EU officials have indeed stated on several occasions that Armenia’s authorities are cooperating with Western partners.
During a US House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee’s hearing in November, Assistant State Secretary James O’Brien praised the reforms undertaken by the Armenian government that allow the US administration to track the trade with Russia.
“In almost real-time, they can see which firms are involved in this circumvention trade, and then we’re able to take measures to stop that trade. It works remarkably well,” he stated.
In March 2024, the European Parliament assessed positively Armenia’s overall record of cooperation in the context of sanctions.
In its resolution on closer ties between the EU and Armenia, the European Parliament noted that despite the increased exports to Russia the EU’s Special Envoy on Sanctions, David O’Sullivan, has not voiced any concern over Armenian authorities’ cooperation with the EU on preventing sanctions circumvention.
“There appears to be a divergence of opinions between the Western expert community and officials from the US and EU on this matter,” Hovhannes Nazaretyan of EVN Report, a prominent Armenian analytical media platform, told Euractiv.
“While some experts occasionally accuse Armenia of attempting to circumvent sanctions, officials from both Brussels and Washington commend Armenia for its transparency in providing information and for its compliance with the requirements of the sanctions regime,” Nazaretyan told Euractiv.
However, despite the positive statements of relevant EU and US bodies specialised in monitoring sanctions implementation, Armenian experts stress the need to monitor both the Armenian government’s policies on sanctions and the media manipulation waves on English language media platforms.

high_priority_articles.title: Deployment of AI Recruitment Tools in the EU: Employer Obligations Under GDPR and EU AI Act - ogletree.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Deployment of AI Recruitment Tools in the EU: Employer Obligations Under GDPR and EU AI Act  ogletree.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Quick Hits
- Spain’s data protection authority, the AEPD, issued a formal warning to a company before its AI recruitment tool was switched on.
- EU regulators demonstrate willingness to invoke their GDPR powers and intervene at the AI procurement stage.
- The EU AI Act lists as high-risk, under Annex III, certain types of AI recruitment tools including those that screen or filter applications, and evaluate candidates throughout the recruitment process.
- High-risk recruitment AI tools trigger human oversight and transparency obligations.
- Noncompliance with the GDPR can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4 percent of global annual turnover for employers.
- Noncompliance with the EU AI Act can attract fines of up to €35 million or 7 percent of global annual turnover for employers.
The AEPD recently issued a formal preventive warning to an organisation that was preparing to deploy an AI recruitment tool that would screen and evaluate job applications, and existing employee applications for internal mobility.
The AEPD acknowledged that AI can improve the efficiency and quality of hiring processes, although it stressed that data protection safeguards must be embedded from the very outset, reflecting the GDPR principle “data protection by design and by default.”
The AEPD highlighted several specific legal requirements when it comes to deploying an AI recruitment tool. Organisations must undertake a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before the tool is used, where the processing is likely to result in a “high risk” to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Candidates and employees must receive clear and comprehensible information about how their personal data will be processed and the role the AI tool will play in evaluating them. Human oversight of outcomes is required by both the GDPR and the EU AI Act. This must be “effective,” meaning the decision-maker must be able to critically assess the score or output generated by the system and reach their own independent conclusion, rather than simply rubber-stamping the AI’s recommendation.
Practical Considerations
For employers wishing to deploy AI recruitment tools that will be used to rank and filter applications, the first step is to determine if the tool will be assisting recruitment decisions or influencing or determining decisions.
The GDPR (Article 22) gives individuals the right not to be subjected to decisions made solely through automated processing that would have a legal or similarly significant effect on them. The AEPD warning showcases how the functioning of an AI recruitment tool, and the level of human-intervention in the process outcomes, will be central to whether or not Article 22 applies.
If the tool will be influencing decisions, employers will need to undertake a DPIA, implement appropriate safeguards, notify individuals that automated decision-making is in use, update privacy notices describing the role of AI in the recruitment process, and ensure there is human oversight and documentation relating to this particular safeguard.
Additionally, the EU AI Act Annex III lists as high-risk AI recruitment tools that screen and filter candidates—this is the case even if the tool does not make the final recruitment decision. This classification means that employers will need to take compliance steps including:
- where applicable, performing a fundamental rights impact assessment;
- establishing a protocol for human oversight which would include the ability for someone to analyse, challenge, and override outcomes, maintain an in-depth understanding of how the AI works (e.g., how it is trained, tested, guardrails in place to minimise risk of bias, can verify and explain outcomes, has in place strong audit controls);
- documenting how the recruitment process relies on AI outcomes;
- providing training to their recruitment team; and
- updating privacy notices to inform individuals that they will be subject to automated decision-making.
Regulatory Action in the EU and the Impact on U.S. Employers
As governments and tech leaders discuss the regulation of AI the AEPD warning illustrates how EU regulators have already acted and are moving earlier and more assertively to enforce data protection and AI governance requirements around automated hiring technology, even before a tool goes live.
The AI recruitment tool in question is the type of cost-saving, efficiency tool that many employers are exploring and deploying. These tools will rapidly scan through applications, assign scores, and prioritise candidates. This strategically significant tech, with sizeable upfront costs, aims to reduce costly recruitment processes by speeding up the labor-intensive steps associated with resume review, and identify the best talent.
For U.S. employers that recruit candidates located in Europe, this is a reminder to build privacy and AI compliance into the recruitment tool procurement process before new recruitment tools are deployed. If the new recruitment tool is screening and filtering applications and candidates, then it is likely high-risk AI under the EU AI Act. If the new recruitment tool is capable of making decisions, rather than simply assisting the employer, it likely meets the automated decision-making threshold of the GDPR. Both legal frameworks impose strict requirements that must be complied with.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Highlights
- The benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield rose 2 basis points to 3.095%.
- Japan's services inflation accelerated at its fastest annual pace in more than two years.
- The two-year JGB yield climbed 1.5 basis points to 1.950%.
- The 30-year JGB yield increased 1 basis point to 4.165%.
- Investors are monitoring upcoming 40-year and two-year JGB auctions for signals on demand and market liquidity.
Japanese Bond Yields Rise Amid Inflation Concerns
Japanese government bond yields moved higher as investors assessed rising services inflation and expectations of further monetary tightening by the Bank of Japan.
The benchmark 10-year JGB yield increased 2 basis points to 3.095%, bringing it closer to levels not seen since the mid-1990s. The rise reflects changing expectations around future interest rates and inflation in Japan.
Services Inflation Raises Policy Expectations
Japan's services inflation accelerated in August at its fastest annual pace in more than two years.
The increase in services prices has added to concerns about persistent inflationary pressures within the economy. Rising inflation can influence expectations for monetary policy and consequently affect demand and pricing across the government bond market.
BOJ Policy Outlook
Minutes from the Bank of Japan's July policy meeting highlighted concerns among policymakers regarding inflation risks.
Some policymakers supported more aggressive interest-rate increases. The BOJ recently raised its benchmark interest rate to 1.25%, reinforcing expectations of continued attention on inflation and monetary policy.
Changing expectations around future rate decisions have contributed to upward pressure on Japanese government bond yields.
Upcoming JGB Auctions in Focus
Market participants are also monitoring upcoming Japanese government bond auctions.
The Ministry of Finance is scheduled to auction 40-year bonds on Tuesday, followed by two-year bonds on Wednesday. Demand at these auctions could provide an indication of investor appetite for Japanese government debt amid elevated yields.
Auction results could also influence yield levels and liquidity across the JGB market.
Two-Year JGB Yield Reaches 1.950%
Short-term Japanese government bond yields also moved higher.
The two-year JGB yield increased 1.5 basis points to 1.950%, matching the peak recorded during the previous week.
Short-term yields are particularly sensitive to expectations surrounding central-bank policy because changes in anticipated interest rates can quickly affect the pricing of shorter-duration government bonds.
Long-Term Yields Continue to Rise
The upward movement extended across the longer end of the JGB yield curve.
The 30-year JGB yield increased 1 basis point to 4.165%. The move reflects continued market attention on inflation, interest-rate expectations and the supply of government debt.
As bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, rising yields indicate that bond prices are facing downward pressure.
What Bond Investors Are Watching
The Japanese bond market remains focused on inflation data, BOJ policy signals and upcoming government bond auctions.
Further economic data could influence expectations around future interest-rate decisions, while auction demand could provide additional indications about investor appetite at current yield levels.
FAQs
Q: Why are Japanese government bond yields rising?
A: JGB yields are rising amid accelerating services inflation and expectations that the Bank of Japan could continue tightening monetary policy.
Q: What is the current 10-year JGB yield mentioned in the article?
A: The benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose 2 basis points to 3.095%.
Q: What happened to the two-year JGB yield?
A: The two-year JGB yield increased 1.5 basis points to 1.950%, matching the previous week's peak.
Q: Why are upcoming JGB auctions important?
A: The 40-year and two-year bond auctions could provide information about investor demand, market liquidity and the potential impact of government bond supply on yields.
Q: What happened to the 30-year JGB yield?
A: The 30-year JGB yield increased 1 basis point to 4.165%, extending the rise across the longer end of the Japanese government bond yield curve.

high_priority_articles.title: How a Chinese ‘smart sex toys’ company fed Russian war tech against Ukraine — and exposed an EU sanctions blind spot - EUobserver
high_priority_articles.summary: How a Chinese ‘smart sex toys’ company fed Russian war tech against Ukraine — and exposed an EU sanctions blind spot  EUobserver
high_priority_articles.full_text:
“It takes years to sanction something that can be replicated in days—so what is the point of sanctions at all?”
This is a question we hear repeatedly in our work at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO) in Ukraine to close gaps in the sanctions regime.
And the frustration behind it is justified: several entities we submitted for designation years ago were added to the EU sanctions list only recently.
Since 2014, the European Union has sanctioned about 3,000 individuals and entities in relation to the war against Ukraine. The US has blacklisted over 7,000.
These lists include, among many others, third-country sanctions-evasion facilitators.
One such network exposed in late 2024 supplied microelectronics and British-made optical equipment later used in Russian military aircraft.
The UK sanctioned it nearly six months later; the EU took almost two years. It is one of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of such cases.
Sanctions take time: authorities must gather evidence, meet legal requirements, and assess their impact. Meanwhile, new companies can replace those under scrutiny, keeping the network running.
The British optics case shows how the main facilitator sourced goods from an alleged Hong Kong supplier of essential oils and confectionery flavourings — at an address shared with several companies already sanctioned for evasion.
(Almost) all roads lead to China
This essential-oils supplier was hardly an isolated curiosity.
It pointed to a wider infrastructure of shared addresses, corporate service providers, and unlikely businesses through which new suppliers can keep appearing as others are sanctioned.
Our study traced roughly 1,800 foreign suppliers and more than $800m [€702m] in trade in priority Western microelectronics—only a fraction of the true scale. Most passed through mainland China and, especially, Hong Kong.
China’s role in sanctions evasion — and the shell companies that help facilitate it — is hardly breaking news. But some suppliers in our dataset run very real businesses in rather unexpected fields.
Fuxin Pharmaceutical makes medicines and agrochemicals — and trades in Western microelectronics. Taibung Piping Equipment sells steel fittings for energy and petrochemical systems, alongside integrated circuits, semiconductors, and power electronics.
Shenzhen NuanQin Technology took things further.
It advertised “smart sex toys” but shipped to Russia no "Leopard Print Beginner’s Floggers" or "OMG! Feather Ticklers".
Customs records show industrial electronics, integrated circuits, and other dual-use components instead.
Its corporate footprint is equally eclectic: NuanQin is also linked to an FPV drone retailer.
Many others have generic names, no websites, and almost no public footprint.
To a Western dual-use manufacturer, they may look like small retailers or freight forwarders — unremarkable enough to pass conventional sanctions screening and keep trading.
Shared addresses are a red flag
Their addresses can reveal what company-by-company screening misses. Sharing one with a sanctioned firm does not warrant automatic designation, but it is a strong signal of diversion risk.
The numbers speak for themselves.
One Hong Kong office unit housed at least 45 companies, with perhaps 20 more: 14 under sanctions or export controls, and 31 unrestricted. Together, they supplied Russia with over $16m in priority microelectronics—within our dataset alone.
Other obscure suppliers lead businesses to claim they sell hats, salon equipment, or even offer immigration services.
Such links may be unsurprising in a world of virtual offices and corporate service providers, but a simple sanctions check misses them, even as tens of millions of dollars in trade pass through.
Beyond the shopfront
Offshore links recur throughout the data. We found 33 addresses associated with offshore structures and used by 66 suppliers, fewer than half of them restricted. Together, those suppliers accounted for over $57m in shipments to Russia, including $26m from unrestricted firms.
A shared office in the British Virgin Islands or Seychelles may raise an obvious red flag. Other connections are much harder to spot.
Take another Hong Kong supplier linked to millions of electronics and microelectronics supplies to Russia. Its ordinary-looking office address has also been used by offshore service providers and operators of tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
A shared address does not prove a coordinated network, but it points to corporate infrastructure serving both chip procurement and oil-sanctions evasion.
An even more striking case leads to Liu Baoxia. The United States sanctioned her in 2017, and the FBI placed her on its wanted list in 2025. Her network smuggled US electronics to Iran for its missile and drone programmes through Hong Kong front companies in the Ho King Commercial Center.
NAKO identified at least 14 companies supplying microelectronics to Russia from those same offices. Only five have been sanctioned.
Follow the address, not the company
Every company in our dataset, sanctioned or not, supplied Russia with priority microelectronics. We found more than 200 addresses linked to restricted entities. Over 450 suppliers used them, accounting for nearly $380m in trade.
Since 2024, the US Bureau of Industry and Security has listed high-risk addresses alongside company names.
Yet address-based screening remains limited, especially outside the United States. The Common High Priority List shows that governments can agree on shared diversion risks.
They should now do the same for addresses, particularly as Russian and Iranian procurement networks appear to use overlapping corporate infrastructure.
A shared list would help governments and manufacturers scrutinise replacement companies before each requires a separate investigation.
An address does not make every tenant guilty by association. But it should stop an ostensibly clean supplier from getting an automatic green light. Sanctions target companies; evasion networks reuse the infrastructure behind them.

high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea Sets Five-Year Push to Double Semiconductor Production, Seeks U.S. Investment for AI Supply Chains  Spherical Insights
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea is stepping up its semiconductor expansion and AI strategy as it seeks to increase chip-production capabilities, attract U.S. investment and build supply chains that are more resilient to external disruptions.
South Korea is entering a new phase of semiconductor expansion as artificial intelligence drives demand for advanced computing, memory and data-centre infrastructure. On September 23, 2026, President Lee Jae Myung announced that the country aims to double semiconductor production capabilities within five years while seeking U.S. investment and stronger AI supply chains resilient to external shocks. The announcement comes as semiconductor exports reach record levels, with August exports rising 209% year over year to $46.65 billion, according to South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. The strategy extends beyond production growth, focusing on AI infrastructure and supply-chain resilience. With Samsung Electronics and SK hynix central to South Korea’s semiconductor industry, the expansion could influence global chip capacity, investment and AI supply chains.
South Korea’s Semiconductor Industry Enters a New Growth Phase
South Korea remains a major global semiconductor manufacturing hub, particularly in memory chips, with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix holding strong positions in DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM has become increasingly important as AI accelerators require faster, higher-capacity memory for training and inference workloads. SK hynix reported that it began mass shipments of HBM4 in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung is also expanding its HBM4 business as AI infrastructure investment accelerates.
The strength of this segment is also visible in South Korea’s trade performance. In August 2026, semiconductor exports reached a record $46.65 billion, rising 209% year over year, with demand supported by AI infrastructure investment from major hyperscalers. Semiconductors therefore remain central to the country’s export economy, while rising demand for advanced memory is increasing the importance of domestic production capacity. South Korea’s broader semiconductor strategy is consequently focused not only on maintaining its memory leadership but also on expanding manufacturing capacity, supporting advanced technologies and strengthening supply-chain resilience.

South Korea’s Double-Production Plan: What Happened?
At the Korea Investment Summit in New York on September 23, 2026, President Lee Jae Myung announced that South Korea would double its semiconductor production capabilities within five years by expanding a chip-production hub. He linked the plan to the country’s three megaprojects, launched earlier in 2026 to develop a semiconductor cluster and other AI facilities. The government also plans to establish a Future Fund to support industrial infrastructure and talent development, while pursuing conditions intended to attract additional global investment. Lee said the strategy would also focus on building critical AI supply chains that are less vulnerable to external shocks.
Why Is South Korea Targeting Higher Semiconductor Production?
Rising AI computing needs are making advanced chips, memory, data centres, and secure supply chains increasingly important to South Korea’s technology strategy.
Rising AI Chip Demand
AI training and inference require increasingly powerful processors and high-performance memory. Expanding domestic semiconductor capacity can help South Korea respond to this growing demand while supporting its broader AI ambitions.
HBM and Advanced Memory Growth
HBM has become a critical component of AI computing because it enables high-speed data movement between processors and memory. South Korea is therefore prioritizing next-generation memory technologies to maintain technological strength as AI workloads become more demanding.
Global Supply-Chain Resilience
Semiconductor production depends on complex international networks for equipment, materials and components. Increasing domestic capacity and developing supporting industries can reduce exposure to disruptions and strengthen Korea’s position within global supply chains.
Growing Data-Center Infrastructure
AI expansion requires large-scale computing infrastructure, creating additional demand for processors, memory, networking and supporting technologies. South Korea’s government has outlined plans for 8.4 GW of AI data-center capacity, with phased operations planned from 2029.
Strategic Technology Competition
Semiconductor leadership is increasingly connected to national competitiveness in AI and other advanced technologies. South Korea is strengthening its ecosystem through support for next-generation semiconductors, AI infrastructure and domestic technology development as competition intensifies globally.
How Is AI Changing South Korea’s Semiconductor Strategy?
AI data centres require powerful GPUs, AI accelerators and high-performance computing systems supported by HBM and advanced packaging. As AI workloads expand, demand is increasing for memory with greater bandwidth and capacity, making advanced semiconductor manufacturing more important. This is pushing South Korea to strengthen AI infrastructure and chip capabilities across processors, memory, packaging and data-centre technologies.
Samsung and SK hynix: What Role Could Korea’s Chip Giants Play?
Samsung Electronics
Samsung combines memory, foundry and advanced semiconductor manufacturing within its chip business. In Q2 2026, its Memory Business reported record quarterly revenue and expanded HBM4 sales, while it also shipped HBM4E samples to major customers. Samsung and Broadcom additionally announced a collaboration spanning memory, foundry and advanced packaging, with an estimated value of more than $200 billion through 2030.
SK hynix
SK hynix is strengthening its position in HBM, AI memory, NAND and advanced packaging. The company reported Q2 2026 revenue of KRW 79.32 trillion and began HBM4 mass shipments during the quarter. It also announced KRW 100 trillion of investment in Cheongju, including KRW 80 trillion for the M17 NAND fab and KRW 20 trillion for the P&T7 advanced-packaging facility.

Top 5 Semiconductor Trends Shaping South Korea’s AI Strategy
HBM Demand Is Rising
AI accelerators require extremely fast memory to process large workloads, making HBM increasingly important. This is encouraging Korean manufacturers to expand advanced-memory production and prepare capacity for longer-term AI demand.
AI Data Centers Are Increasing Chip Requirements
Large AI data centers require GPUs, memory, networking chips and other semiconductor components. Growing AI infrastructure is therefore expected to increase demand across South Korea’s semiconductor ecosystem.
Advanced Packaging Is Becoming More Important
As AI chips become more complex, packaging increasingly affects performance, power efficiency and memory integration. South Korea plans to develop Chungcheong as an advanced packaging hub, with KRW 81 trillion in planned investment.
Domestic Semiconductor Capacity Is Expanding
Companies are committing substantial capital to new fabrication facilities. SK hynix, for example, announced approximately KRW 54 trillion for new DRAM and NAND fabs in Yongin and Cheongju, with cleanroom openings planned for 2029 and 2028 respectively.
Supply-Chain Security Is Becoming a Strategic Priority
Semiconductor production depends on a broad network of materials, equipment, components and manufacturing facilities. South Korea is therefore developing multiple regional production and support hubs to diversify capacity and strengthen the resilience of its semiconductor value chain.

high_priority_articles.summary: UK Considers Chinese EV Tariffs During EU Trade Discussions  Fuel Cells Works
high_priority_articles.full_text:
• The UK government is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as London seeks access to proposed “Made in Europe” measures amid reported EU pressure for closer alignment on Chinese EV tariffs.
• Britain does not impose the additional anti-subsidy duties introduced by the EU on Chinese-made EVs, while the UK automotive industry is warning that exclusion from “Made in Europe” measures could put an €80 billion [$94 billion] annual UK-EU automotive trading relationship at risk.
Britain is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as it seeks access for UK manufacturers to the European Union's proposed “Made in Europe” industrial measures.
UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said tariffs on Chinese EVs were “under review” and described the government's position as “finely balanced,” with different parts of Britain's automotive industry seeking different approaches.
“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” Reynolds told Politico at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool.
His comments come as London seeks to ensure British manufacturers are not excluded from the EU's proposed “Made in Europe” measures.
The Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the discussions, that EU officials have pressed Britain to align more closely with the bloc's trade policy, including by raising tariffs on Chinese vehicles. The reported tariff linkage has not been publicly announced by the European Commission.
The UK did not follow the EU when Brussels imposed additional countervailing duties on battery-electric vehicles imported from China in 2024.
EU duties currently range from 7.8% to 35.3%, depending on the manufacturer, on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Britain has not introduced equivalent additional anti-subsidy duties on Chinese EVs.
The issue has become more prominent as Chinese brands increase their UK market share. Chinese-made vehicles account for around 16% of UK new-car sales this year, according to figures cited in reporting on the EU-UK discussions.
The discussions come as the EU works on its Industrial Accelerator Act and proposed “Made in Europe” provisions.
The legislation is intended to support European production through measures including public procurement and industrial support. Britain is concerned that UK-built vehicles and other products could fall outside parts of the framework.
Reynolds said excluding British industry would not serve the EU's objective of strengthening European manufacturing.
“The Made in Europe push is supposed to be about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds said. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders is also pressing for UK-built vehicles to be included.
Oxford Economics analysis commissioned by SMMT estimates that UK automotive production supports around €24 billion [$28 billion] of spending on EU-produced goods and services, 250,000 EU jobs and significant tax revenues.
The UK-EU automotive trading relationship is worth about €80 billion [$94 billion] annually, according to SMMT. Britain is the EU's largest export market for passenger cars, while the EU is Britain's largest passenger-car export market. The UK is also the largest importer of EU-built automotive components.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said excluding British manufacturers from the proposed measures would reduce demand for EU-made components and affect manufacturers on both sides.
SMMT wants UK-produced vehicles to be treated as “assembled in the EU” for the purposes of the proposed rules.
The UK government has not committed to introducing additional tariffs on Chinese EVs.
Higher duties would bring British policy closer to the EU's approach but could expose UK exporters to Chinese retaliation and affect Britain's efforts to attract Chinese automotive investment.
Reynolds said those considerations are part of why the government regards the decision as finely balanced.

United States President Donald Trump has forcefully denied reports that his administration offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets in exchange for concessions on its nuclear program. The denial follows an investigative report detailing active backchannel negotiations between Washington and Tehran, highlighting the intense friction between clandestine diplomatic efforts and the public posturing required to manage domestic political narratives and regional alliances.
The mechanics of frozen assets and sanctions relief
The disputed report alleged that American negotiators proposed a framework wherein Iran would halt the advanced enrichment of uranium and cooperate with international inspectors in return for the unfreezing of billions of dollars in sovereign assets held in third-party jurisdictions. These funds, largely accumulated from oil sales prior to the reimposition of maximum pressure sanctions, are currently sequestered in financial institutions across Asia and the Middle East, subject to strict US Treasury waivers that limit their use to humanitarian goods.
Releasing these funds requires complex multilateral coordination. Any formal sanctions relief would necessitate navigating the "snapback" mechanism embedded in United Nations Security Council resolutions, a process that European allies have previously threatened to trigger if Iran's nuclear latency crosses specific thresholds. Consequently, backchannel discussions often focus on informal administrative waivers and the quiet non-enforcement of secondary sanctions on regional oil buyers, rather than the formal dismantling of the statutory sanctions architecture that the executive branch cannot easily reverse without congressional approval.
Domestic politics versus backchannel diplomacy
The President's swift and categorical rejection of the report underscores the severe domestic political liabilities associated with engaging Tehran. In the current political environment, any perceived concession to Iran is rapidly weaponized by opposition lawmakers and regional allies who view the Islamic Republic as the primary architect of Middle Eastern instability. By publicly declaring that no such offer was made, the administration attempts to insulate itself from accusations of appeasement, even as intelligence and diplomatic officials continue to explore avenues to prevent a nuclear breakout.

This dynamic creates a persistent paradox in US-Iran relations: the executive branch requires plausible deniability to conduct negotiations, yet the strategic signaling required to deter Iranian escalation often leaks to the press, forcing public denials that can simultaneously derail the very talks they are meant to conceal. Diplomatic veterans note that such public disavowals are standard operating procedure in high-stakes nuclear negotiations, where the mere acknowledgment of an offer can collapse the fragile domestic consensus required for the other side to accept it.
The legacy of the JCPOA and the snapback mechanism
The current diplomatic paralysis is inextricably linked to the collapse of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. Following the US withdrawal from the accord in 2018 and the subsequent reimposition of sweeping economic sanctions, Iran incrementally breached the treaty's limits on uranium enrichment and heavy water stockpiles. Today, the original framework is effectively defunct, leaving diplomats attempting to negotiate a "less for less" interim agreement that freezes Iran's most advanced nuclear activities in exchange for limited, phased access to its sequestered oil revenues.
Complicating these efforts is the looming threat of the UN snapback mechanism, a provision in Security Council Resolution 2231 that allows any participating state to unilaterally reimpose all pre-2015 international sanctions. European powers have repeatedly warned that Iran's refusal to cooperate with the International Atomic Energy Agency could trigger this mechanism, which would legally obligate even reluctant US allies to enforce a global embargo. This legal sword of Damocles serves as the primary leverage for Western negotiators, even as public political narratives demand a posture of maximum pressure rather than diplomatic compromise.
Constraints on Iran's nuclear program and regional fallout
Beyond the political optics, the substance of the alleged negotiations points to the narrowing window for a diplomatic solution. Iran's stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium has expanded significantly since the collapse of the 2015 nuclear accord, reducing the breakout time to a matter of weeks. Any credible agreement would require Tehran to physically dilute or export this stockpile, a concession that the Iranian supreme leadership has historically resisted without immediate, verifiable, and substantial economic relief.
- Enrichment Caps: Demands for Iran to dismantle advanced centrifuge cascades at the Natanz facility.
- Inspection Access: Restoring IAEA monitoring cameras and granting snap inspections of undeclared sites.
- Regional Proxy Restraint: Linking nuclear concessions to the curtailment of ballistic missile transfers to allied militias.
Regional actors, particularly Israel and the Gulf states, remain deeply skeptical of any bilateral arrangement between Washington and Tehran that lacks ironclad security guarantees. They argue that sanctions relief merely provides the Iranian state with the liquidity required to fund regional proxies and accelerate its conventional military programs. As the UN nuclear watchdog continues to report on Tehran's non-compliance, the gap between the public denials of diplomatic outreach and the urgent reality of the nuclear timeline continues to widen, leaving the region in a state of precarious, unmanaged escalation.

high_priority_articles.summary: Canada’s Asia Trade Strategy: What Could Near-Complete ASEAN and Philippines Deals Mean for Canadian Exporters and TSX Stocks?  kalkine.ca
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Highlights
- Canada says separate free-trade negotiations with ASEAN and the Philippines are more than 90% complete.
- Ottawa is targeting progress toward final agreements around November.
- The trade push is part of Canada's broader strategy to diversify international economic relationships.
- Energy, particularly LNG, is being positioned as a major Canadian offering to Southeast Asia.
- Critical minerals, agriculture, technology and infrastructure could also benefit from deeper trade ties.
- Canada is exploring Investment opportunities in the Philippines, including the Luzon Economic Corridor.
- Data centres and digital infrastructure are emerging as additional areas of cooperation.
- Energy, Mining, Industrials, Technology, Utilities, Transportation and Financials could be relevant TSX sectors.
Why Is Canada’s ASEAN Trade Push Trending?
Canada is accelerating its economic engagement with Southeast Asia as Ottawa seeks to expand the number of markets available to Canadian businesses.
Canada's Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said on September 22 that negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Philippines are more than 90% complete, with Ottawa aiming to have the agreements ready around Prime Minister Mark Carney's planned November visit to Manila.
The development is significant because Southeast Asia is becoming an increasingly important manufacturing, technology and consumer region.
For Canada, deeper relationships could create additional markets for natural resources, agricultural products, technology and industrial goods.
Why Is ASEAN Important to Canada?
ASEAN represents a major regional economic bloc comprising 10 Southeast Asian economies.
The region has a large and growing consumer base and is deeply integrated into global Manufacturing Supply chains.
Countries across Southeast Asia are investing heavily in infrastructure, energy, technology and industrial capacity.
This creates several potential opportunities for Canadian companies.
Canada's objective is not simply to increase exports.
Ottawa is also seeking investment partnerships and supply-chain relationships that can connect Canadian businesses with broader Asian markets.
What Is the Philippines Opportunity?
The Philippines is becoming increasingly important within Canada's Asia strategy.
The country has a large population, growing infrastructure requirements and an expanding digital economy.
Canada is also exploring opportunities connected to the Luzon Economic Corridor, which links major economic and industrial areas.
Potential investment areas include infrastructure, logistics, energy and digital services.
A completed trade agreement could provide a broader framework for Canadian businesses seeking to establish commercial relationships in the country.
Could LNG Become Canada’s Biggest Asian Export Opportunity?
Energy is one of the clearest potential areas of opportunity.
Canada's Pacific coast LNG infrastructure provides a route to Asian customers.
The Canadian government has identified growing LNG capacity as a major asset when engaging with Southeast Asian economies seeking to diversify energy supplies.
For Canadian energy companies, Asian Demand could provide additional markets beyond North America.
The commercial impact will depend on LNG prices, long-term contracts, shipping costs, infrastructure capacity and production levels.
Could Southeast Asia Become a Major Canadian Energy Market?
Potentially.
Several Southeast Asian economies are expanding their electricity systems and industrial bases.
Natural gas can play a role in electricity generation and industrial activity.
Canadian LNG could therefore become part of a broader regional energy-diversification strategy.
However, Canada faces competition from established LNG suppliers located closer to Asian markets.
Transportation distance and shipping Economics will remain important.
Why Are Critical Minerals Important?
Critical minerals could become another major component of Canada-ASEAN economic relations.
Southeast Asia is developing manufacturing capacity in areas such as batteries, electronics and advanced industrial products.
These industries require reliable supplies of metals and minerals.
Canada has significant deposits of minerals relevant to electrification and advanced manufacturing.
Stronger trade and investment relationships could therefore connect Canadian Mining companies with Asian industrial customers.
Could Mining Companies Gain New Customers?
Potentially.
Canadian mining companies often seek long-term customers and financing partners when developing major projects.
Asian manufacturers can provide demand for metals such as copper, nickel and other industrial minerals.
The opportunity could extend beyond raw-material exports.
Canada could seek investment in processing and refining capacity, creating greater domestic value before materials are exported.
Could Agriculture Benefit?
Agriculture is another important Canadian export opportunity.
Southeast Asian economies have growing food demand and significant Import requirements.
Canadian producers could potentially expand sales of grains, pulses, meat and other agricultural products.
Better trade access could also help exporters diversify away from concentrated markets.
However, tariffs, food standards, logistics and local competition will influence the commercial impact.
Could Canadian Technology Companies Benefit?
Technology is becoming a larger component of Canada's International Trade strategy.
Southeast Asian economies are investing heavily in:
- Artificial intelligence
- Data centres
- Cloud infrastructure
- Cybersecurity
- Digital payments
- Telecommunications
- Software
- Advanced manufacturing
Canadian technology businesses could potentially enter these markets through partnerships and direct investment.
The Philippines in particular has a large services and technology sector that could create opportunities for Canadian companies.
Why Are Data Centres in Focus?
The growth of AI and digital services is increasing demand for data centres across Asia.
Data centres require substantial electricity, cooling systems, telecommunications infrastructure and construction.
Canada's technology and energy expertise could potentially support these developments.
The opportunity also creates potential cross-border investment opportunities for Canadian infrastructure and financial companies.
Could Infrastructure Investment Increase?
Southeast Asia is undertaking major infrastructure development.
Ports, railways, airports, roads, power systems and digital networks require significant capital.
Canadian engineering, construction and financial companies could potentially participate.
The Luzon Economic Corridor is one area where Canada is exploring investment opportunities.
Such projects could create demand for Canadian expertise in engineering, infrastructure finance and technology.
Could Financial Institutions Benefit?
Trade expansion generally creates additional demand for financial services.
Canadian banks and other financial institutions could support:
- Export financing
- Corporate lending
- Project finance
- Currency management
- Investment banking
- Cross-border transactions
- Trade finance
If Canadian companies increase their presence in Southeast Asia, financial institutions could potentially expand alongside them.
How Does This Fit Canada’s Trade Diversification Strategy?
Ottawa has repeatedly described diversification as a long-term objective.
The government says the Southeast Asia push is not simply a response to U.S. trade policy.
Instead, Canada wants to build stronger relationships with multiple international markets regardless of developments elsewhere.
This is important because Canada remains heavily integrated with the U.S. economy.
Diversification takes years and requires new infrastructure, Business relationships and supply chains.
Trade agreements can provide the framework for that process.
Could Canada Reduce Its Dependence on the U.S.?
A complete shift would be difficult because North American trade is deeply integrated.
However, Canada can potentially increase the share of exports and investment directed toward other markets.
Southeast Asia offers one potential source of diversification.
Europe and other Indo-Pacific economies are also part of Ottawa's broader strategy.
The goal is therefore better understood as expanding Canada's international Options rather than replacing existing relationships.
Could the Agreements Affect TSX Energy Stocks?
Energy companies could be among the sectors most sensitive to developments.
Higher long-term LNG exports could potentially support production and infrastructure investment.
Pipeline and transportation infrastructure could also see additional demand.
However, investors need to monitor actual contracts rather than simply trade negotiations.
An agreement creates market access, but companies still need to secure customers and build commercially viable projects.
What Could This Mean for TSX Investors?
Energy: LNG producers and infrastructure companies could gain additional international-market opportunities.
Mining: Critical-mineral producers could develop relationships with Asian manufacturers.
Agriculture: Canadian food and agricultural exporters could access additional consumers.

In separate posts on X, Misri said he met US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg and Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker, with the engagements covering key areas of India-US bilateral cooperation.
"Great to meet Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg in New York. Agreed to advance India-U.S. cooperation in critical and emerging technologies, including through Pax Silica, and strengthen cooperation in semiconductors and critical minerals," Misri said.In another post, the Foreign Secretary said he discussed energy security and several other strategic issues with Hooker.
"A productive meeting with Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker in New York today. Discussed various elements of India-US bilateral cooperation, including energy security and the recently enacted SRIA, civil nuclear cooperation, TRUST and the Indian Ocean Strategic Venture initiative," he said.
India-US cooperation in areas considered strategically important to economic and national security, including supply-chain resilience, advanced technologies and energy.
Pax Silica, launched in December 2025 by Helberg, is the US State Department's flagship initiative focused on AI and supply-chain security. The initiative seeks to build cooperation among partner countries around secure and innovative supply chains spanning critical minerals, energy inputs, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors and AI infrastructure.
The initiative has also expanded its membership. At the 2026 Summit, Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, El Salvador, the European Union, Germany, Greece, Kazakhstan, the Netherlands and Panama joined the Pax Silica Declaration. The new additions brought the number of signatories to 24, alongside Australia, Finland, India, Israel, Japan, Norway, Qatar, South Korea, Singapore, Sweden, the Philippines, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Taiwan has separately endorsed the declaration's principles through a joint statement on US-Taiwan economic security cooperation.The broader cooperation under Pax Silica has also included discussions on artificial intelligence and supply chain security. The United States and nearly three dozen Pax Silica economies signed a Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, with participants including India, Australia, Argentina, Germany, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Against this backdrop, Misri's meeting with Helberg assumes significance for India's engagement with Washington on critical minerals and semiconductor supply chains, as both countries seek to deepen cooperation in strategic technologies and strengthen resilience in areas vulnerable to supply disruptions.
Misri's meeting with Hooker, meanwhile, covered energy security as well as the SRIA, civil nuclear cooperation, TRUST and the Indian Ocean Strategic Venture initiative.The discussion on SRIA comes as India continues to assess the implications of US legislation targeting Russia's energy trade and countries purchasing Russian oil and gas.
The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, or SRIA, provides a statutory framework for expanded sanctions, import duties and trade restrictions concerning Russia, while also extending economic measures relating to Iran. The legislation focuses on areas including Russia's petroleum and military sectors, government officials, financial institutions and vessels associated with efforts to circumvent restrictions on Russian crude exports.
For India, the legislation has particular relevance because it creates a potential mechanism under which Washington could impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on imports from countries that continue purchasing Russian energy, subject to the statutory conditions and any subsequent invocation by the US President Donald Trump.The legislation itself, however, does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on Indian goods. Rather, it provides the executive branch with authority to impose such tariffs under specified conditions.
India and China remain among the major purchasers of Russian crude, making the issue of continued energy trade with Moscow an important component of the wider discussion over sanctions and global energy markets.
New Delhi has maintained that its energy-security decisions are guided by national interests and market considerations. The Ministry of External Affairs has also said India is closely monitoring developments concerning the legislation and remains determined to protect its trade and economic interests.

The two-year JGB yield, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for the Bank of Japan's policy rate, rose as high as 1.975% on Monday, its highest level since March 1995. The yield has doubled over the past 12 months and is more than six times its level at the same point in 2024.
Read more: Global Market: Nikkei falls as oil surge, global bond selloff rattle markets
The move comes amid a broader global rise in bond yields as higher energy prices and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure fuel inflation concerns. In Japan, however, the rise has been amplified by expectations that the BOJ could adopt a more hawkish stance to support the yen.
Markets price in further BOJ tightening
The BOJ raised its key policy rate to 1.25% earlier this month, the highest level in 31 years. Despite the increase, the yen has remained under pressure, adding to concerns that imported inflation could persist.
Markets are increasingly pricing in the possibility of consecutive BOJ rate increases. Dai-ichi Life Research Institute chief economist Koichi Fujishiro said the combination of political and diplomatic pressure was making investors more alert to the prospect of further hikes.
Yen weakness adds to inflation concerns
The yen's persistent weakness has become a key concern for Japanese policymakers because it raises the cost of imported goods and energy.
Reuters reported that analysts increasingly expect the BOJ's policy focus to include limiting the inflationary impact of a weaker currency. The pressure comes despite the latest rate increase and recent warnings from Japanese and U.S. officials.
Japan's fiscal position is another factor complicating the outlook. Government debt remains more than twice the size of annual economic output, while rising borrowing costs are increasing debt-servicing expenses.
Read more: Global Market: RoboTechnik slides below IPO price in weak Hong Kong debut
Longer-term yields climb
The rise in Japanese bond yields has extended beyond the front end of the curve. Japan's five-year government bond yield touched a record 2.43% on Monday, while the one-month interest-rate swap rate starting in two years, viewed by market participants as an indicator of the potential endpoint of the BOJ's tightening cycle, climbed to a record 2.5%.
Money-market pricing points to a 36% probability of the BOJ raising its policy rate to 1.5% in October, according to Tokyo Tanshi. Traders have fully priced such a move for December.
Tankan report in focus
The timing of the next rate increase could depend on economic data, particularly the BOJ's Tankan survey of business sentiment among major manufacturers, due on Thursday.
A strong reading on capital investment could strengthen the case for an October rate increase, according to Resona Asset Management chief fund manager Takashi Fujiwara.
The sharp rise in short-term yields therefore signals that markets are reassessing how far Japan's rate cycle may ultimately extend, with inflation, yen weakness, corporate investment and fiscal pressures all shaping expectations for the BOJ's next moves.

Bank of England (BoE) Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden said on Monday that risks to the inflation outlook have become increasingly tilted to the upside, according to Reuters.
Ramsden said he remains focused on external pressures from energy prices, weather and Artificial Intelligence (AI) supply chains, alongside domestic risks from food prices and potential second-round effects.
The BoE policymaker added that if upside inflation pressures continue to build, there could be a case for raising the bank rate. However, Ramsden does not expect the central bank to consider further Quantitative Easing (QE) anytime soon.
Ramsden flags upside inflation risks, keeping GBP supported
BoE’s Ramsden scores 8.4/10 on FXS Speechtracker, notably above the historic 7.1/10 baseline, signalling a stronger-than-usual policy impact. The focus on external inflation pressures from energy, weather and AI-related supply chains, alongside domestic indirect effects in food prices and potential second-round effects, marks a clear hawkish tilt.
By stating that risks to the inflation outlook have shifted to the upside and that continued upside pressures could justify increasing Bank Rate, Ramsden reinforces expectations that the BoE may need to keep policy tight or even re-tighten. This hawkish bias is supportive for GBP, especially against the Euro and Dollar, as markets reassess the probability of renewed rate hikes or a prolonged high-rate stance.
Market reaction
The British Pound (GBP) shows no significant reaction to Ramsden’s hawkish comments. GBP/USD remains higher, gaining 0.21% on Monday to trade around 1.3250 at the time of writing.
BoE FAQs
The Bank of England (BoE) decides monetary policy for the United Kingdom. Its primary goal is to achieve ‘price stability’, or a steady inflation rate of 2%. Its tool for achieving this is via the adjustment of base lending rates. The BoE sets the rate at which it lends to commercial banks and banks lend to each other, determining the level of interest rates in the economy overall. This also impacts the value of the Pound Sterling (GBP).
When inflation is above the Bank of England’s target it responds by raising interest rates, making it more expensive for people and businesses to access credit. This is positive for the Pound Sterling because higher interest rates make the UK a more attractive place for global investors to park their money. When inflation falls below target, it is a sign economic growth is slowing, and the BoE will consider lowering interest rates to cheapen credit in the hope businesses will borrow to invest in growth-generating projects – a negative for the Pound Sterling.
In extreme situations, the Bank of England can enact a policy called Quantitative Easing (QE). QE is the process by which the BoE substantially increases the flow of credit in a stuck financial system. QE is a last resort policy when lowering interest rates will not achieve the necessary result. The process of QE involves the BoE printing money to buy assets – usually government or AAA-rated corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Pound Sterling.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE, enacted when the economy is strengthening and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the Bank of England (BoE) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to encourage them to lend; in QT, the BoE stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive for the Pound Sterling.

The FINANCIAL — NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte will travel to Münster, Germany, on October 1 for meetings with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, as European intelligence agencies warn that Russia may intensify its campaign against NATO countries.
Rutte will also visit the 1st German-Netherlands Corps and deliver a speech at the 2026 International Westphalian Peace Prize ceremony. The visit comes less than three weeks after Rutte said Germany was playing a leading role in NATO’s military transformation and after NATO publicly backed Berlin following what Germany described as a Russian hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
On September 24, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service said Russia was likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, with potentially greater consequences for targeted countries. It assessed a “low but growing risk” of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. The service said an outright invasion remained highly unlikely, although it could not be ruled out.
Days earlier, Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka told The Guardian that a limited Russian incursion, false-flag operation or major influence campaign could occur within “months, not years.” Baltic intelligence officials have taken a more cautious position, saying they see no evidence of an imminent attack.
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said the alliance was increasing intelligence sharing in response to suspected Russian sabotage and other incidents.
Why Germany, France and Italy
Russia’s apparent strategy is lweakening the political and military coalition supporting Ukraine. Germany is particularly important because of its role in NATO logistics, military production and assistance to Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has described the Leipzig incident as part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression against Europe.
Germany plans to spend €124.7 billion on defense-related military capabilities in 2026, equivalent to about 2.7% of GDP. The government expects military spending to reach at least 3.5% of GDP by 2029, with defense-related infrastructure adding another 1.5%.
France presents a different target. It is a nuclear-armed NATO member and one of Europe’s principal military powers. French authorities have documented Russian-linked information operations aimed at influencing political debate and undermining confidence in democratic institutions.
Italy is strategically important because of its Mediterranean position and role in NATO. In July, Italy expelled two Russian military attaches accused of espionage.
A September 24 report in Spain’s El Mundo, cited by ANSA, said U.S. intelligence had identified alleged Russian plans for drone attacks against France, Italy and Spain, potentially using drones launched from ships and concealed in containers. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the alert had not been confirmed by Italian authorities. The report therefore remains an allegation rather than an established operational threat.
European intelligence assessments point to several potential Russian objectives: disrupting military assistance to Ukraine, forcing European governments to spend more on domestic security, creating political divisions and testing whether NATO members would respond collectively to a limited attack.
Recent events have given NATO a growing list of potential scenarios. Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle incident. Poland has investigated suspected sabotage affecting a Starlink facility supporting Ukrainian military communications. NATO has increased intelligence sharing in response.
The historical memory behind Europe’s response
Eastern Europe’s concern about Moscow also has a long historical foundation.
After World War II, the Soviet Union established political and military dominance across much of Central and Eastern Europe. Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising in 1956 and led the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 after Alexander Dubček’s government introduced reforms.
The Soviet Union also occupied and incorporated Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940, an annexation the United States refused to recognize.
The Warsaw Pact, created in 1955, brought the Soviet Union together with Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania, Albania and East Germany in a Soviet-led military alliance.
For the Baltic states and countries such as Poland, Russia’s current pressure is therefore viewed through a history in which Moscow previously used military force to maintain a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe.
Ukraine remains the center of the confrontation
Russia is conducting sustained missile and drone attacks against Ukraine while Ukraine has expanded strikes against Russian military and energy infrastructure. At the same time, European governments are increasing military spending and strengthening NATO’s eastern defenses.
Germany has permanently stationed a new armored brigade in Lithuania, while the 1st German-Netherlands Corps has taken a new command role on NATO’s eastern flank.
The result is a widening contest between Russia and NATO that increasingly extends beyond the battlefield.
For Rutte, Merz and Jetten, the October 1 meetings in Münster are likely to focus on how NATO can deter Russia, protect European infrastructure and maintain support for Ukraine while avoiding escalation into a direct NATO-Russia war.
RIA Novosti’s Deleted Lithuania Article Raises New Questions Over Russian Threats
A Russian state news agency briefly published an article on September 25 describing a potential conflict with NATO member Lithuania as another Russian “special military operation” and suggesting that Moscow could use nuclear-armed missiles. RIA Novosti deleted the article several hours later, saying it did not reflect the views of its editorial board, its editorial policy or Russian state policy.
The article, written by Alexander Nosovich, editor-in-chief of the Kaliningrad-based pro-Russian outlet RuBaltic.Ru, was titled “Russia Is In for Another SVO. It Will Be Very Short.” It appeared after Lithuania’s parliament advanced a proposal to remove the country’s constitutional prohibition on stationing nuclear weapons and foreign military bases.
Lithuania’s September 22 parliamentary vote was 99-13, with five abstentions. The vote did not itself authorize nuclear weapons or foreign bases in Lithuania; it advanced a constitutional change that would require further votes.
Nosovich argued that a conflict in the Baltic region would be much shorter than Russia’s war in Ukraine because of geography. He wrote that Russia could potentially avoid deploying ground forces and instead use missiles “with the appropriate warhead,” explicitly introducing a nuclear-strike scenario.

India reserves third-party rights in Russia-EU CBAM trade dispute in WTO
India has reserved its third-party rights in a WTO dispute filed by Russia against the European Union over its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, allowing New Delhi to follow the proceedings
Listen to This Article
India, along with several other countries, has reserved its third-party rights to participate in proceedings related to a trade dispute filed by Russia against the European Union over its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body has agreed to establish a panel to adjudicate the issue, an official said.
 
Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, Chinese Taipei, Indonesia, Japan, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand, the UK and the US are other countries that have reserved their third-party rights in the dispute, the Geneva-based official said.
 
Russia has filed a dispute against the EU's CBAM package and alleged export subsidy under the EU scheme for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances.
 
The WTO Dispute Settlement Body, at its meeting in Geneva on Friday, agreed to set up a panel to adjudicate the matter, the official said.
 
Another official said becoming a third party in the case will help India follow the proceedings in the dispute.

"This is a constructive step for India as it will allow the country to see what is happening in the dispute. It can see the EU's as well as Russia's stand on the matter," the official added.
 
Third-party status would enable India to present its views on the WTO issues raised by Russia without becoming a principal party to the dispute.
The case is important for India because exporters of carbon-intensive products such as steel and aluminium face additional compliance requirements, including carbon costs and taxes, under the EU's CBAM regime.
